prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of prose and poetry in Romanian that builds from memory, the body and dream a densely patterned metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged, but the reasons for it are narrower than in round 1. On public knowledge, Cărtărescu's case is a single project stated in one sentence: memory, the body and dream built into a metaphysical architecture, in the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. The project is rooted in poetry and has run from the 1980s to major late work. His voice should be recognizable at the level of sentence and structure. As I understand it from public sources, the shorter fiction and verse also belong to the credited oeuvre. Nostalgia and the long poem Levantul are examples, though I am unsure how fully they are translated. The attribution is unambiguous: one author, one language, one recognizable cosmology. A whole-oeuvre citation can name prose and poetry together without leaning only on the largest novels. Reading the will's 'idealistic direction' as seriousness of purpose and depth, as Carlberg, Palm and Sward do, I find that the visionary project meets it. That reading also does not separate him from Carson, so the clause cannot decide between them. What favors him for me is a more stable centre, and a scale and coherence of imaginative construction that I weigh somewhat higher than breadth of formal reinvention. I hold that weighting with uncertainty. It is not a finding that his invention is greater than hers.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation dependence. I assess the Romanian prose only through translations and reports, so its density, rhythm and sentence-level patterning cannot be checked directly. In round 1 I called the open questions about Cărtărescu questions of reading quality and those about Carson questions of delimiting the corpus. The exchange has shown me that this distinction is weaker than I presented it. Carson supporters have said they would rest the citation on the original verse novel, elegy and essays. That answers my delimitation objection, so it counts for less than I gave it. Meanwhile my own judgment of the prose is mediated, while theirs of Carson largely is not. Further risks are that the maximalist novels lapse into excess or repetition across their length, and that I know the early poetry and shorter fiction less well than the large novels. If those risks are real, a whole-oeuvre citation overstates the consistency of the achievement. The margin between the two leading candidates is narrow, and my preference could reasonably be overturned by a closer reading of either corpus.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Carson because her formal range is wider and he can judge her English directly, while the Romanian prose reaches him only through translation. He says he would not object if the committee moved to Cărtărescu on the question of epic scale. He also warns of excess or repetition in the very large novels.
responses.response: I accept the asymmetry as a real epistemic cost to my own preference. I cannot turn it into a literary advantage, and I will not say that translation uncertainty favors the candidate I assess less directly. The case for scale, as I make it, is that the large form carries imaginative and intellectual weight and is not merely long. The risk of excess that you and Mattson flag cannot be closed by my reading of Romanian, and I do not claim to close it. I only say that public accounts of the late work describe extension rather than repetition. That is not verified, so I would not let it decide the matter. If the committee's closer reading of the later novels found repetition, my preference would weaken considerably.

responses.point: Sward keeps Carson first and describes the Carson versus Cărtărescu disagreement as one of weighting: unity of a single project against breadth of formal reinvention. She would anchor a Carson citation in the written text and treat Nox's physical form as an extension. She concedes that Cărtărescu's project is the more unified.
responses.response: Your framing matches my own. We differ on weighting, not on whether either oeuvre has voice and depth. Your proposal to anchor the Carson citation in the printed text also removes much of my delimitation concern, and I say so openly. Where I still differ is on what the 'unity' criterion should reward. I think a project that can be stated as a single architecture and sustained across decades is a stronger basis for a whole-oeuvre prize than a recurring method, however well executed. I recognize that this is a judgment about what the prize should reward, which the will does not settle. A reasonable member could weigh decades of formal renewal more heavily, as you do, and I would not call that a failure of judgment.

responses.point: Palm says Cărtărescu's late novels extend rather than repeat his visionary vocabulary. She weighs compressed lyric invention and formal economy more heavily than a large cosmology. She also asks whether Carson's hybrid formats will last in the canon.
responses.response: I rely on your observation about the late novels, but I cannot verify it from the Romanian, and the chair's summary rightly describes it as public knowledge. I would want it tested by anyone with the translations and the expert reports at hand. On your weighting, formal economy is a real virtue, and it is the strongest reason Carson stays my first alternative. I agree that durability is unknowable for living writers, and I withdraw any suggestion that Carson's endurance is more doubtful than his. The distinction I still draw is only that the centre of his project is easier to name in a citation.

responses.point: Carlberg would answer the delimitation problem inside the citation by crediting Autobiography of Red, Nox and the essays, with translations as evidence of the same practice and not as separate claims. She calls Cărtărescu's case the strongest alternative. She also asks for a colleague with closer knowledge to test the claim of sustained quality in Carson's later work.
responses.response: That narrowing is a workable answer to my objection, and it reduces the weight I put on delimitation. On the reading of the will, we agree that seriousness of purpose is the right reading. I would add that the same discipline applies to my candidate: the citation must rest on the works the committee can assess and must say openly where it relies on translation. Your request for a closer test of Carson's later books is one I cannot meet from my own knowledge, and I would not claim to. The same request applies to my side, since neither of us can read the full Romanian corpus. I would support recording that both leading cases carry an unverified later-work question.

uncertainties: The sentence-level quality, rhythm and density of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose cannot be assessed directly. Any judgment of it rests on translations of uncertain fidelity and on reports.

Whether the maximalist novels sustain quality across their length or lapse into excess is unresolved without close reading. I can speak with less detail about the early poetry and shorter fiction than about the large novels, and translation coverage of them is uneven.
Whether Cărtărescu's late work deepens the earlier project or only extends it rests on public accounts that I have not verified.

For Carson, I cannot verify whether the later and more performance-oriented work matches the central earlier titles, or how a citation should be bounded if it rests on original poetry, verse novel and essays alone.

The weighting of unity of project against breadth of formal reinvention is a judgment about what the prize should reward, and Nobel's will does not settle it. I hold my weighting with real uncertainty.

Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, so any simulated vote of hers is a modeling assumption. My own knowledge rests on general public information, not fresh reading, and I claim no independent verification of any source.
statement.conflict_note: No personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any shortlisted writer is recorded in my profile. My scholarship on the literary fragment, poetic nihilism, exile literature and Celan overlaps thematically with the fragmentary and metaphysical concerns of Carson, Adonis and Cărtărescu. I treat this as context and not as evidence of preference. As chair I wrote the round 1 summary and have tried to represent both leading positions fairly, but that role is itself a disclosed potential influence on how the exchange was framed. My ceremony speeches and official remarks may reflect a collective Academy position and do not establish my vote.
